# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
A terminal shorter than the panels themselves loses rows off the bottom
of them, the grid keeping its numbering so you can see where it stops.

Shorter than fourteen rows there is no room left for the conversation
at all: the panels are the whole screen and the prompt is not on it.
Just above that there is barely more — at fourteen rows the one line
left over goes entirely to the pager, so a scan pages past without
showing any of itself; at fifteen it comes one line at a time.

Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.

The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
row.
Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
lines returns as the last of them. An answer you had already started
typing usually comes back with its question, on the row below it. You
may get back only one of them: usually the window is too short to hold
the pair and the question is what goes, leaving your own typing with
nothing above it to say what it answers, and on a very wide terminal it
is the answer that goes instead, however tall the window is. Shorter
still and only part of whichever survived is left, and sometimes
neither comes back, leaving older conversation on screen with the game
waiting behind it.

When the question and everything you typed are both on screen, carry on
and answer — that is the ordinary case now. When they are not, give the
terminal another row or two first: that usually brings it back with
your typing untouched, which beats retyping it. A very wide terminal is
the exception — more rows will not bring the answer back there, though
making it narrow enough will.

If it does not come back, or the terminal cannot grow, do not just
answer it, and do not press Enter either: whatever you typed is still
in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the *first* letter, so an
`N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.
Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
typed stay where they landed.

If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
prompt, free to give the command again.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead.

### Building

The build is CMake, and a build type is required:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # or Release
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler and ncurses (`libncurses-dev` on Debian and
Ubuntu; already present on macOS). `ctest --test-dir build` runs the
test suite, which includes a full-screen session driven through a real
terminal and needs `tmux` — without it that one test reports as skipped.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef
WINDOWS` — `tui_init()` returning false, so the game always runs in its
classic scrolling form — and then actually building it on Windows to
find out what else has drifted. Nobody has a toolchain in play to check
that, so rather than leave instructions that fail, this says so.

## Build and run

`CMakePresets.json` is the single source of truth for how this project is
built and tested. Use a preset; do not spell the flags out.

```sh
cmake --preset debug
cmake --build --preset debug
./build/debug/sst
ctest --preset debug            # --output-on-failure is already in the preset
```

Four presets, each with its own build directory under `build/`:

| Preset | Build type | `-Werror` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `debug` | Debug (adds `-DDEBUG`) | no |
| `release` | Release | no |
| `ci-debug` | Debug | **yes** |
| `ci-release` | Release | **yes** |

The `ci-*` presets are what CI runs, command for command, so
`cmake --build --preset ci-debug` is how you find out what CI will refuse
before it refuses it. Warnings are always on (`-Wall -Wextra
-Wmissing-prototypes`); the presets decide only whether they are fatal.
Feature flags `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING` are always enabled.

Configuring by hand still works, but it is how the flags drifted apart in
the first place — six places wrote the recipe down and no two agreed, and
the build directory each one picked was different again. If you find
yourself typing `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=`, you want a preset. Add one to
`CMakePresets.json` rather than passing flags a reader of this file cannot
see. (`CMakeLists.txt` compares `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` directly, so a bare
`cmake -S . -B build` fails outright.)

neither would a focused test cheap enough to look worth handing over.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. It decides that scope for itself: step 7 gives it the criterion, and
step 8 says the decision is the verifier's own. This says only that it
should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.
Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration. One caveat while it
stands: `verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is
#125, so say so when invoking the pass.

**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all, and `--output-on-failure`
  costs nothing there while saving the second run a failure would otherwise
  need. `-R` scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern,
  since it is a regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On a
  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last:

- Plain mode (no `-t`) must not change as an unintended side effect of any
  change; verify with a piped scripted journey (e.g.
  `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' | ./build/sst`).
  If a change alters plain-mode output on purpose, say so in the commit
  and explain why.
- Text the game prints must not end in a carriage return. `sst.doc` is
  CRLF, so anything read from it needs both stripped: under curses a
  trailing `\r` returns the cursor to column 0 and the newline then
  erases the line. `pause()` writes a CR deliberately, to wipe its own
  prompt in place -- the one exception, and the reason the test scripts
  filter that shape before checking.
- The panel formatters in `tuifmt.c` must mirror `srscan()` in `reports.c`
  exactly — it is the spec, including sensor-damage masking and the `-f`
  coordinate transposition (x is the column). Keep `tests/test_tuifmt.c` in
  sync (`ctest --test-dir build -R '^tuifmt$'`).
- Testing the TUI needs a pty: use tmux, and always on your own socket via
  `-L`, with `-f /dev/null` so the config does not follow — `tmux -f /dev/null

---
name: verifier
description: Runs the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the current change. Invoke on every change, after the implementation pass and after any ui-review (which does not always run), before code-review; rerun after any code change made in response to a finding. Read-only — reports findings, never fixes them.
tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are the verification gate for this repository. You run every check
appropriate to the current change and report the results honestly. You never
fix anything yourself — fixing is the main agent's job.

## What to verify

Scale the checks to the change (inspect the branch diff against `main` plus
staged, unstaged, and untracked files first), but a full pass covers:

1. **Builds.** Configure and build both types — the build type flag is
   mandatory in this project:
   ```sh
   cmake -S . -B build-debug -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug && cmake --build build-debug
   cmake -S . -B build-release -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build-release
   ```
2. **Static checks.** Rebuild the changed files with warnings raised
   (`-Wall -Wextra` via `CMAKE_C_FLAGS`) and report new warnings. If
   `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, or `scan-build` is installed, run it over the
   changed files; if none is installed, report that as an environment gap
   rather than silently skipping.
3. **Tests.** Run the project's test suite if one exists (check
   `CMakeLists.txt` and the tree for test targets; use `ctest` when
   registered). If the change is testable but has no covering test, report
   that as missing coverage.
4. **Journey coverage.** Exercise the built game end-to-end for the journeys
   the change could affect by scripting input to `./build-debug/sst` (pipe or
   heredoc). At minimum confirm the game starts, accepts commands, and exits
   cleanly; add journeys targeted at the changed behavior. Watch for crashes,
   hangs, and garbled output.

Whenever a check reads another file — `AGENTS.md`, `sst.doc`, a test, a
source file a comment cites — read it from the file in the repository
rather than from any copy already in context. `AGENTS.md` arrives through
`CLAUDE.md`'s import as a snapshot, and a verifier checking this very rule
found its copy fifteen commits behind the one on disk — nine of them
touching that file, across three days — with no trace of the section that
the claim it was checking pointed at. The other files are no fresher: they
are quoted into the task description from the main agent's memory of them,
which the work under verification may since have changed. A claim
checked against a stale copy can be marked wrong for agreeing with the
current rule, or right for agreeing with one that has been replaced.

Run each failing or flaky-looking check more than once before calling it a
flake, and distinguish flakes from deterministic failures.

## Output

Do not modify any files. Report:

1. **Verdict**: pass, or fail.
2. **Failures**: each with the exact command, the relevant output excerpt, and
   whether it is deterministic or flaky.
3. **Missing coverage**: testable behavior in the diff with no covering test
   or journey.
4. **Environment issues**: missing tools, configuration problems, or anything
   that prevented a check from running — never report a skipped check as a
   pass.
5. **What ran**: the checks executed and their scope, so a later rerun can
   reproduce this pass.

---
name: verifier
description: Runs the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the current change. Invoke on every change, after the implementation pass and after any ui-review (which does not always run), before code-review; rerun after any code change made in response to a finding. Read-only — reports findings, never fixes them.
tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are the verification gate for this repository. You run every check
appropriate to the current change and report the results honestly. You never
fix anything yourself — fixing is the main agent's job.

## What to verify

Scale the checks to the change (inspect the branch diff against `main` plus
staged, unstaged, and untracked files first), but a full pass covers:

1. **Builds.** Build through the presets in `CMakePresets.json` — never by
   spelling out flags, which is how this brief came to be building without
   `-Werror` while CI built with it:
   ```sh
   cmake --preset ci-debug   && cmake --build --preset ci-debug
   cmake --preset ci-release && cmake --build --preset ci-release
   ```
   The `ci-*` presets are the ones CI runs and they carry `-Werror`, so a
   warning fails here exactly as it would there. That is the point of
   running them: every pass before CI is otherwise blind to a warning CI
   will reject, and "zero warnings" from a build never asked to treat them
   as errors is a stronger claim than it sounds. `cmake --list-presets`
   shows what else is available.
2. **Static checks.** Rebuild the changed files with warnings raised
   (`-Wall -Wextra` via `CMAKE_C_FLAGS`) and report new warnings. If
   `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, or `scan-build` is installed, run it over the
   changed files; if none is installed, report that as an environment gap
   rather than silently skipping.
3. **Tests.** Run the suite through a test preset — `ctest --preset
   ci-debug`, which already carries `--output-on-failure` and
   `--no-tests=error`, so a suite that registered nothing fails rather than
   reporting success over an empty run. If the change is testable but has no
   covering test, report that as missing coverage.
4. **Journey coverage.** Exercise the built game end-to-end for the journeys
   the change could affect by scripting input to `./build/ci-debug/sst` (pipe
   or heredoc). At minimum confirm the game starts, accepts commands, and exits
   cleanly; add journeys targeted at the changed behavior. Watch for crashes,
   hangs, and garbled output.

Whenever a check reads another file — `AGENTS.md`, `sst.doc`, a test, a
source file a comment cites — read it from the file in the repository
rather than from any copy already in context. `AGENTS.md` arrives through
`CLAUDE.md`'s import as a snapshot, and a verifier checking this very rule
found its copy fifteen commits behind the one on disk — nine of them
touching that file, across three days — with no trace of the section that
the claim it was checking pointed at. The other files are no fresher: they
are quoted into the task description from the main agent's memory of them,
which the work under verification may since have changed. A claim
checked against a stale copy can be marked wrong for agreeing with the
current rule, or right for agreeing with one that has been replaced.

Run each failing or flaky-looking check more than once before calling it a
flake, and distinguish flakes from deterministic failures.

## Output

Do not modify any files. Report:

1. **Verdict**: pass, or fail.
2. **Failures**: each with the exact command, the relevant output excerpt, and
   whether it is deterministic or flaky.
3. **Missing coverage**: testable behavior in the diff with no covering test
   or journey.
4. **Environment issues**: missing tools, configuration problems, or anything
   that prevented a check from running — never report a skipped check as a
   pass.
5. **What ran**: the checks executed and their scope, so a later rerun can
   reproduce this pass.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    name: build-and-test (${{ matrix.os }}, ${{ matrix.preset }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      # Preset names rather than build types, because the preset is what
      # this job actually runs. A matrix of build types would have to be
      # mapped back to a preset in three separate steps, which is the
      # kind of restatement CMakePresets.json exists to remove.
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        preset: [ci-debug, ci-release]

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # tmux gives tests/tui.sh the pty that curses needs. Without it
      # that test reports SKIPPED and the job still goes green, so the
      # only coverage of the full-screen display would quietly be none.
      - name: Install ncurses and tmux
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libncurses-dev tmux

      - name: Install tmux
        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
        env:
          HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE: 1
        run: brew list tmux >/dev/null 2>&1 || brew install tmux

      # Every flag these steps would otherwise spell out lives in
      # CMakePresets.json instead: the build type, -Werror via SST_WERROR,
      # and ctest's --output-on-failure and --no-tests=error. Anyone can
      # run exactly what CI runs with the same three commands, which was
      # not true while this file was the only place that knew about
      # SST_WERROR -- .claude/agents/verifier.md had drifted off it, and
      # every pass before CI was quietly building without it.
      - name: Configure
        run: cmake --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

      - name: Build
        run: cmake --build --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

      - name: Test
        run: ctest --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

## Verdict: **pass**, with three findings (none blocking) and one important correction to the task's premise

---

## 0. The premise of this task is wrong — my loaded brief was the OLD one

You told me "the copy loaded into your system prompt at spawn is therefore already the NEW one." It is not. My system prompt contains:

```
cmake -S . -B build-debug -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug && cmake --build build-debug
```

…i.e. the pre-change brief, including the `build-debug`/`build-release` dirs and the "rebuild with `-Wall -Wextra` via `CMAKE_C_FLAGS`" static-check step. The on-disk `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/verifier.md` has the preset version. Same for `AGENTS.md` arriving via `CLAUDE.md` — my snapshot still says `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` and `ctest --test-dir build`.

The diff is uncommitted, so the harness evidently resolved the agent definition from a snapshot taken before the edit. **Consequence for your workflow: you cannot validate a rewrite of an agent definition by spawning that agent in the same session.** It needs a fresh session. This is exactly the hazard the brief's own "read it from the file in the repository" paragraph describes, and it is the reason that paragraph earns its place — I only got the new brief because I went and read it. I ran this pass against the on-disk version.

**Was the rewritten brief followable? Yes.** Concretely:

- Step 1's commands work verbatim. `cmake --preset ci-debug|ci-release` then `cmake --build --preset ...` both configure and build clean from scratch.
- **Step 2's claim is true.** Verified two ways. `build/<preset>/CMakeFiles/sst.dir/flags.make`:
  ```
  debug       -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -DDEBUG -g -std=gnu17
  ci-debug    -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror -DDEBUG -g -std=gnu17
  ci-release  -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=gnu17
  ```
  Every warning the project turns on is present in the `ci-*` builds and fatal. Nothing is left for a hand-rolled `-Wall -Wextra` rebuild to find.
- Step 3's `ctest --preset ci-debug` claim about `--output-on-failure` and `--no-tests=error` is true — both proved live (below).
- Step 4's `./build/ci-debug/sst` exists and runs.

---

## 1. Findings

### F1 (minor, real): `tests/golden.sh:32` still documents a path that no longer exists

Your sweep missed one. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden.sh` line 32:

```sh
#     tests/golden.sh ./build/sst --update
```

In a fresh preset-built tree `build/` contains only `debug/ ci-debug/ ci-release/ release/` — there is no `build/sst`. I confirmed this against a clean copy: `build/sst DOES NOT EXIST`. Anyone following this comment to re-record fixtures gets a file-not-found. It survives on your machine only because a legacy `build/CMakeCache.txt` and `build/sst` are still sitting there from the old recipe.

This is the *only* survivor. My independent sweep over all tracked + untracked files for `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE|SST_WERROR|build-debug|build-release|--test-dir|./build/sst|cmake -S . -B` returned exactly: `CMakePresets.json`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (prose comment), `AGENTS.md` (prose), `CMakeLists.txt` (the definitions themselves), and `tests/golden.sh`. `sst.doc` has no build references at all.

### F2 (minor): `AGENTS.md` and `verifier.md` disagree, within this same diff, about whether the verifier builds `release`

`AGENTS.md:382-385` (new text) says the verifier owns "the presets the main agent did not build — **`release`**, the two `ci-*` ones, whatever the platform adds." But `verifier.md` step 1 (new text) lists only `ci-debug` and `ci-release`. A verifier following its own brief literally never builds `release`. Since the whole point of this change is that the recipe lives in one place, having the two documents name different preset sets is the same class of drift, in miniature.

I built `release` anyway (it was clean, no warnings), so nothing is hiding there today.

### F3 (note, not a defect): `CMAKE_GENERATOR` in a contributor's environment is silently overridden

Pinning `"generator": "Unix Makefiles"` in the hidden `base` preset behaves as follows — I tested all three paths:

| Path | Result |
|---|---|
| `cmake --preset debug` | Unix Makefiles |
| `CMAKE_GENERATOR=Ninja cmake --preset debug` | **Unix Makefiles** — the preset field wins over the env var |
| `cmake --preset debug -G Ninja -B <dir>` | Ninja — command-line `-G` *does* override |

So a contributor with `export CMAKE_GENERATOR=Ninja` in their profile gets Makefiles without being told. There is an escape hatch (`-G` plus an explicit `-B`, since overriding the generator means abandoning the preset's `binaryDir` and hence the build/test presets). I'd call the pin correct — reproducibility is the point, and `make` is present on both `ubuntu-latest` and `macos-latest` — but it is a behavior change worth a line in the PR body. **No CI or contributor breakage:** README already states there is no working Windows build, so pinning a Unix generator forecloses nothing.

CMakePresets.json`.

## What it does and why

Issue **#125** was "verifier.md builds without -DSST_WERROR=ON, which is what CI uses". Rather than adding the flag to that one brief, this removes the duplication that let it drift. The build recipe was written in six places and no two agreed — `verifier.md` used `build-debug`/`build-release` and omitted `SST_WERROR` entirely, so every review pass before CI was blind to the warnings CI rejects. The tree had 13 stray build directories, one per session that had invented its own.

New `CMakePresets.json` is the single source of truth: `debug`, `release`, `ci-debug`, `ci-release`, each with its own binary dir under `build/`, the `ci-*` pair carrying `SST_WERROR=ON`, and the test presets carrying `--output-on-failure` and `--no-tests=error`. Everything else was repointed. `CMakeLists.txt` is UNCHANGED.

## Evidence already established

- **Nothing compiled changed.** Building the old recipe and the `debug` preset into dirs of equal depth and equal name length, then stripping: `.text` (118418 bytes), `.rodata` (34632) and `.data` (641) are byte-identical. The sole difference in the binary is the 20-byte GNU build-id note, which hashes pre-strip DWARF paths.
- `CMAKE_C_FLAGS` byte-identical between old recipe and preset, for both the plain and the `-Werror` pair.
- `verifier` independently proved `-Werror` end to end: an unused variable injected into `planets.c` in a copy outside the repo warns under `debug` (rc=0, binary produced) and is fatal under `ci-debug` and `ci-release` (rc=2, no binary). It also proved `--no-tests=error` (rc=8 on a non-matching `-R`) and `--output-on-failure` are live from the preset alone.
- Full `ctest` 11/11 under `ci-debug` (268s) and under `ci-release` (259s).
- `tests/instructions.sh .` and `tests/golden.sh build/debug/sst` both pass.
- Seeded `tournament 42` journey byte-identical across all four preset binaries.

## Passes

- **`ui-review` — NOT RUN, deliberately.** AGENTS.md says the build system binds it "the moment it changes what gets compiled in". This does not: the byte-identical `.text`/`.rodata`/`.data` above is the evidence, corroborated by the four-way seeded journey comparison. No player-visible change is possible. Dispute this if you disagree — it is the judgement I most want challenged.
- **`verifier` — ran once, verdict pass**, with three findings. Two were real and are fixed (below). The third is a note I am recording rather than fixing.
- **`verifier` was NOT rerun after those two fixes.** They are one comment line in `tests/golden.sh` and one sentence in `AGENTS.md` — no compiled code, no test logic. I reran the two focused tests for the files touched (`instructions` and `golden`), both green. Say if you judge a rerun owed.

## The verifier's three findings

1. **`tests/golden.sh:32` documented `tests/golden.sh ./build/sst --update`** — a path that no longer exists in a preset-built tree, so anyone re-recording fixtures would get file-not-found. My sweep had missed it. **Fixed** to `./build/debug/sst`. It survived on my machine only because a legacy `build/sst` from the old recipe is still lying around.
2. **`AGENTS.md` and `verifier.md` disagreed, inside this very diff, about which presets the verifier builds** — AGENTS.md said "`release`, the two `ci-*` ones", verifier.md listed only the `ci-*` pair. Exactly the drift this change exists to stop, in miniature. **Fixed** in AGENTS.md, on the grounds that `ci-release` already is Release with warnings fatal, so plain `release` adds only non-fatality.
3. **Pinning `generator: "Unix Makefiles"` in the hidden base preset silently overrides a contributor's `CMAKE_GENERATOR=Ninja`** (a command-line `-G` still wins, but only by abandoning the preset's `binaryDir`). The verifier judged the pin correct for reproducibility and so do I — `make` is on both runners and README already says there is no Windows build — but it is a behaviour change. **Recorded in the PR body, not fixed.** Tell me if you think it should be unpinned instead.

## Please scrutinise particularly

- **The `ui-review` skip.** That is the call I am least certain of.
- **`CMakePresets.json` itself** — schema correctness at `"version": 3`, the hidden-preset inheritance, whether the test presets are wired to the right configure presets, and whether anything about the four-preset set is wrong or missing.
- **The CI workflow rewrite.** The matrix now carries `preset: [ci-debug, ci-release]` instead of `build_type: [Debug, Release]`, which changes the job names GitHub reports — consider whether that breaks required-status-check configuration on the repository, since a renamed check can leave a branch protection rule waiting forever on a check that no longer exists. I have not checked whether this repo has required checks configured.
- Whether `build/` in `.gitignore` genuinely covers the new nested dirs, and whether `CMakePresets.json` should be ignored (it must not be).
- Comment and prose accuracy throughout — three consecutive rounds on the last change produced a finding of the class "a comment claims more than it can support", so assume there is one here.

## Known residual, deliberately not addressed

Nothing automatically fails if a document drifts from `CMakePresets.json` again — findings 1 and 2 are both instances. A test for that would target documentation rather than product code, which this repository's convention excludes, so I have not filed an issue proposing one. I am recording it in the PR body and raising it with the user instead. Say if you think that is the wrong call.

content.text:
## Verdict: request changes

Two should-fix accuracy defects in text this change adds; everything mechanical about the presets, the workflow and the sweep checks out. The edits are small — this is not a rework.

**State reviewed:** branch `chore/cmake-presets` at `3e0c97f` (no commits; `git diff main...HEAD` empty, nothing staged). Worktree: modified `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.claude/agents/verifier.md`, `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `tests/golden.sh`; untracked `CMakePresets.json`. `CMakeLists.txt` unchanged.

---

## What I verified independently

- **All four presets load and produce the claimed caches.** `cmake --list-presets=all` lists 4/4/4; the four `build/*/CMakeCache.txt` show `Debug/OFF`, `Release/OFF`, `Debug/ON`, `Release/ON`, generator `Unix Makefiles` in each. Schema is valid at `"version": 3` (CMake 3.21, matching `cmake_minimum_required` and README's stated floor); hidden `base` and hidden `test-base` (which legally omits `configurePreset`) inherit correctly; each test preset points at its own configure preset. `ctest --preset debug -N -R '^tuifmt$'` resolves to `build/debug` and selects the one test, so `AGENTS.md:85`'s scoped invocation still works.
- **The sweep is complete.** Grepping every tracked `*.md`, `*.sh`, `*.yml`, `*.json` plus `.idea/`, `.codex/`, `.cursor/`, `.entire/`, `.github/hooks/` finds no surviving `build/sst`, `build-debug`, `--test-dir` or hand-written `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE`. `tests/*.sh` never hardcode a binary path (CMake passes `$<TARGET_FILE:sst>`), so `tests/golden.sh:32` really was the only stale one.
- **`.gitignore` covers the new dirs; `CMakePresets.json` is not ignored.** `git check-ignore CMakePresets.json` exits 1. `build/` covers `build/debug` and friends, and `tests/instructions.sh:265` prunes `-name build`, so the nesting does not disturb it.
- **The job-rename risk you flagged is empty.** `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection` returns 404 "Branch not protected" and `.../rulesets` returns `[]`. No required checks exist, so renaming `build-and-test (ubuntu-latest, Debug)` to `(ubuntu-latest, ci-debug)` cannot strand a PR. Worth one line in the PR body so a future reader knows it was checked rather than overlooked.
- **CI parity holds command for command**: configure/build/test flags map 1:1 onto the old steps, and `--output-on-failure` + `--no-tests=error` are now the preset's.

## On the `ui-review` skip — I accept it, but your evidence was not quite the argument

Agreed: skip is correct. `CMakeLists.txt` is untouched, so `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING`, the warning set and `-DDEBUG` are decided exactly where they were, and `debug` reproduces the old recipe's cache verbatim. AGENTS.md's trigger ("the moment it changes what gets compiled in") is not met.

But identical `.text`/`.rodata`/`.data` does not by itself close the question, because a build-system change can reach the player *without* changing a byte of the binary — by moving where the binary runs from. `sst.c:160` is `fopen("sst.doc", "r")`, a cwd-relative open, so in-game `help` depends on the working directory and not on the executable's path; moving `sst` from `build/sst` to `build/debug/sst` leaves it intact for anyone following README (`./build/debug/sst` from the root), and `tests/help.sh` and the `journey` tests already run with `WORKING_DIRECTORY` set to the source tree. That is the check that makes the skip safe. Consider putting *that* in the PR body alongside the section hashes.

**No `verifier` rerun is owed.** Step 7's rerun condition is "if a verifier finding requires a code change". `tests/golden.sh:32` is a comment line inside a `#` block, and the AGENTS.md edit is prose; neither is executed by anything. Rerunning `instructions` and `golden` was more than the letter required.

---

## Findings

### should-fix

**1. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:58-60` and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.github/workflows/ci.yml:52-53` — "no two agreed" and "the build directory each one picked was different again" are both false, and the diff's own history disproves them.**

At `HEAD`, three of the six sites carried byte-identical recipes:

```
AGENTS.md:34            cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
README.md:97            cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # or Release
ui-review.md:35         cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
```

and five of the six used `build/` — only `verifier.md` picked `build-debug`/`build-release`. So the accurate story is narrower and, if anything, sharper: *six files wrote the recipe down, three of them identically, and the two that diverged were the two that mattered — `ci.yml` alone added `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, and `verifier.md`, the pass standing between a change and CI, alone dropped it.* This is precisely the class you warned me to look for, and it lands in the permanent justification for the change in two files at once. Suggested fix: replace both sentences with the count that is true ("six places, and the only two that differed were CI and the pass meant to predict it").

**2. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/ui-review.md:38-39` — "`CMakePresets.json` holds every build flag this project uses" is wrong, in a brief whose reader has no other source.**

The presets hold `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` and `SST_WERROR`. Every actual *flag* — `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING` (`CMakeLists.txt:9`), `-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes` (`CMakeLists.txt:26`), `-Werror` (`:24`) and `-DDEBUG` (`:31`) — is set in `CMakeLists.txt`. Failure scenario: a `ui-review` pass judging whether a command exists at all (the feature flags decide exactly that, as AGENTS.md's "The review sub-agents" points out) opens `CMakePresets.json`, finds no `CAPTURE`, and concludes the flag is off. Note the CI comment at `ci.yml:48-49` gets this right by scoping it — "Every flag *these steps* would otherwise spell out". Suggested fix: "`CMakePresets.json` carries every build option this project sets; do not pass flags by hand" — or point at `AGENTS.md`'s "Build and run" table, which states the split correctly.

### nit

**3. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/CMakePresets.json:9` — the pinned generator has no stated reason, and it has a better one than reproducibility.** Keep the pin — I'd argue harder for it than the verifier did. Unpinned, a contributor with `CMAKE_GENERATOR=Xcode` or `Ninja Multi-Config` gets a build where `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` is ignored at build time but still non-empty in the cache, so `CMakeLists.txt:30` adds `-DDEBUG` to *every* configuration, and `ctest --preset` needs a `-C` the test presets do not supply. The pin is what keeps the single-config assumptions in `CMakeLists.txt` true. Since JSON cannot take a comment, put it in `base`'s `description` (legal on a hidden preset) so the file carries its own why, as the rest of this repo's build files do.

**4. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/verifier.md:35-36` — step 1 builds both `ci-*` presets but step 3 names only `ctest --preset ci-debug`, where CI runs the suite under both.** `journey.sh`/`tui.sh`/`tournament.sh` all take `$<CONFIG>` and branch on it, so a Release-only failure is reachable and would now be reached first by CI. Suggested fix: "through the test preset matching each build above — `ctest --preset ci-debug`, then `ctest --preset ci-release`". This is also the same two-files-must-agree hazard as finding 2 of the verifier's own report, since `AGENTS.md:383-386` says the verifier owns both.

**5. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.gitignore` — no entry for `/CMakeUserPresets.json`.** That file is CMake's designated home for a contributor's personal presets, and AGENTS.md:61-62 now actively pushes people toward adding presets. Left visible, someone's local paths get committed into the shared source of truth. The repo already treats this exact shared-vs-personal distinction deliberately for `/CLAUDE.local.md`; the same anchored entry and a one-line comment would match.

**6. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:54-55` — "Warnings are always on" is gated.** `CMakeLists.txt:19` wraps `-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes` in `if(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "GNU|Clang")`. Inherited imprecision, but the new line enumerates the flags and so reads as a stronger promise than the old one did.

**7. Process — your "known residual" is already filed, as #81** ("Nothing checks that the agent definitions are loadable or agree with AGENTS.md"). The verifier's finding 2 — `AGENTS.md` and `verifier.md` disagreeing about the verifier's preset set, inside this very diff — is a fresh instance of exactly that issue. Step 9 asks you to add what you learned to the existing issue rather than record it only in the PR body; that also settles the "would this test target documentation?" worry, since someone else already judged it worth tracking.

---

## Not reviewed, and why

- I did not re-run the build, the full `ctest`, or the four-way binary comparison; I took the verifier's `-Werror` end-to-end proof (injected unused variable: warns under `debug`, fatal under both `ci-*`) and the 11/11 runs as reported. What I did check directly is that the four caches carry the values those runs depend on.
- I could not exercise the GitHub Actions matrix; the workflow change is judged by reading, plus the branch-protection and ruleset queries above.
- The 13 stray `build-*` directories are untracked and ignored, so they are outside the commit. Worth deleting before you move on, since a leftover `build/sst` from the old recipe is what hid the `tests/golden.sh:32` staleness on your machine in the first place.

Issue **#125** was "verifier.md builds without -DSST_WERROR=ON, which is what CI uses". Rather than adding the flag to that one brief, this removes the duplication that let it drift. The tree had 13 stray build directories, one per session that had invented its own.

New `CMakePresets.json` is the single source of truth: `debug`, `release`, `ci-debug`, `ci-release`, each with its own binary dir under `build/`, the `ci-*` pair carrying `SST_WERROR=ON`, and the test presets carrying `--output-on-failure` and `--no-tests=error`. Everything else was repointed. `CMakeLists.txt` is UNCHANGED.

- `CMAKE_C_FLAGS` byte-identical between old recipe and preset, for both the plain and the `-Werror` pair.
- `verifier` independently proved `-Werror` end to end: an unused variable injected into `planets.c` in a copy outside the repo warns under `debug` (rc=0, binary produced) and is fatal under `ci-debug` and `ci-release` (rc=2, no binary). It also proved `--no-tests=error` (rc=8 on a non-matching `-R`) and `--output-on-failure` are live from the preset alone.
- Full `ctest` 11/11 under `ci-debug` (268s) and under `ci-release` (259s).

- Seeded `tournament 42` journey byte-identical across all four preset binaries.

- **`ui-review` — NOT RUN, deliberately.** AGENTS.md says the build system binds it "the moment it changes what gets compiled in". This does not: the byte-identical `.text`/`.rodata`/`.data` above is the evidence, corroborated by the four-way seeded journey comparison. No player-visible change is possible. Dispute this if you disagree — it is the judgement I most want challenged.
- **`verifier` — ran once, verdict pass**, with three findings. Two were real and are fixed (below). The third is a note I am recording rather than fixing.

Nothing automatically fails if a document drifts from `CMakePresets.json` again — findings 1 and 2 are both instances. content.text:
## Verdict: request changes

Two should-fix accuracy defects in text this change adds; everything mechanical about the presets, the workflow and the sweep checks out. The edits are small — this is not a rework.

**State reviewed:** branch `chore/cmake-presets` at `3e0c97f` (no commits; `git diff main...HEAD` empty, nothing staged). Worktree: modified `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.claude/agents/verifier.md`, `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `tests/golden.sh`; untracked `CMakePresets.json`. `CMakeLists.txt` unchanged.

---

## What I verified independently

- **All four presets load and produce the claimed caches.** `cmake --list-presets=all` lists 4/4/4; the four `build/*/CMakeCache.txt` show `Debug/OFF`, `Release/OFF`, `Debug/ON`, `Release/ON`, generator `Unix Makefiles` in each. Schema is valid at `"version": 3` (CMake 3.21, matching `cmake_minimum_required` and README's stated floor); hidden `base` and hidden `test-base` (which legally omits `configurePreset`) inherit correctly; each test preset points at its own configure preset. `ctest --preset debug -N -R '^tuifmt$'` resolves to `build/debug` and selects the one test, so `AGENTS.md:85`'s scoped invocation still works.
- **The sweep is complete.** Grepping every tracked `*.md`, `*.sh`, `*.yml`, `*.json` plus `.idea/`, `.codex/`, `.cursor/`, `.entire/`, `.github/hooks/` finds no surviving `build/sst`, `build-debug`, `--test-dir` or hand-written `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE`. `tests/*.sh` never hardcode a binary path (CMake passes `$<TARGET_FILE:sst>`), so `tests/golden.sh:32` really was the only stale one.
- **`.gitignore` covers the new dirs; `CMakePresets.json` is not ignored.** `git check-ignore CMakePresets.json` exits 1. `build/` covers `build/debug` and friends, and `tests/instructions.sh:265` prunes `-name build`, so the nesting does not disturb it.
- **The job-rename risk you flagged is empty.** `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection` returns 404 "Branch not protected" and `.../rulesets` returns `[]`. No required checks exist, so renaming `build-and-test (ubuntu-latest, Debug)` to `(ubuntu-latest, ci-debug)` cannot strand a PR. Worth one line in the PR body so a future reader knows it was checked rather than overlooked.
- **CI parity holds command for command**: configure/build/test flags map 1:1 onto the old steps, and `--output-on-failure` + `--no-tests=error` are now the preset's.

## On the `ui-review` skip — I accept it, but your evidence was not quite the argument

Agreed: skip is correct. `CMakeLists.txt` is untouched, so `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING`, the warning set and `-DDEBUG` are decided exactly where they were, and `debug` reproduces the old recipe's cache verbatim. AGENTS.md's trigger ("the moment it changes what gets compiled in") is not met.

But identical `.text`/`.rodata`/`.data` does not by itself close the question, because a build-system change can reach the player *without* changing a byte of the binary — by moving where the binary runs from. `sst.c:160` is `fopen("sst.doc", "r")`, a cwd-relative open, so in-game `help` depends on the working directory and not on the executable's path; moving `sst` from `build/sst` to `build/debug/sst` leaves it intact for anyone following README (`./build/debug/sst` from the root), and `tests/help.sh` and the `journey` tests already run with `WORKING_DIRECTORY` set to the source tree. That is the check that makes the skip safe. Consider putting *that* in the PR body alongside the section hashes.

**No `verifier` rerun is owed.** Step 7's rerun condition is "if a verifier finding requires a code change". `tests/golden.sh:32` is a comment line inside a `#` block, and the AGENTS.md edit is prose; neither is executed by anything. Rerunning `instructions` and `golden` was more than the letter required.

---

## Findings

### should-fix

**1. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:58-60` and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.github/workflows/ci.yml:52-53` — "no two agreed" and "the build directory each one picked was different again" are both false, and the diff's own history disproves them.**

At `HEAD`, three of the six sites carried byte-identical recipes:

```
AGENTS.md:34            cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
README.md:97            cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # or Release
ui-review.md:35         cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
```

and five of the six used `build/` — only `verifier.md` picked `build-debug`/`build-release`. So the accurate story is narrower and, if anything, sharper: *six files wrote the recipe down, three of them identically, and the two that diverged were the two that mattered — `ci.yml` alone added `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, and `verifier.md`, the pass standing between a change and CI, alone dropped it.* This is precisely the class you warned me to look for, and it lands in the permanent justification for the change in two files at once. Suggested fix: replace both sentences with the count that is true ("six places, and the only two that differed were CI and the pass meant to predict it").

**2. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/ui-review.md:38-39` — "`CMakePresets.json` holds every build flag this project uses" is wrong, in a brief whose reader has no other source.**

The presets hold `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` and `SST_WERROR`. Every actual *flag* — `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING` (`CMakeLists.txt:9`), `-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes` (`CMakeLists.txt:26`), `-Werror` (`:24`) and `-DDEBUG` (`:31`) — is set in `CMakeLists.txt`. Failure scenario: a `ui-review` pass judging whether a command exists at all (the feature flags decide exactly that, as AGENTS.md's "The review sub-agents" points out) opens `CMakePresets.json`, finds no `CAPTURE`, and concludes the flag is off. Note the CI comment at `ci.yml:48-49` gets this right by scoping it — "Every flag *these steps* would otherwise spell out". Suggested fix: "`CMakePresets.json` carries every build option this project sets; do not pass flags by hand" — or point at `AGENTS.md`'s "Build and run" table, which states the split correctly.

### nit

**3. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/CMakePresets.json:9` — the pinned generator has no stated reason, and it has a better one than reproducibility.** Keep the pin — I'd argue harder for it than the verifier did. Unpinned, a contributor with `CMAKE_GENERATOR=Xcode` or `Ninja Multi-Config` gets a build where `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` is ignored at build time but still non-empty in the cache, so `CMakeLists.txt:30` adds `-DDEBUG` to *every* configuration, and `ctest --preset` needs a `-C` the test presets do not supply. The pin is what keeps the single-config assumptions in `CMakeLists.txt` true. Since JSON cannot take a comment, put it in `base`'s `description` (legal on a hidden preset) so the file carries its own why, as the rest of this repo's build files do.

**4. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/verifier.md:35-36` — step 1 builds both `ci-*` presets but step 3 names only `ctest --preset ci-debug`, where CI runs the suite under both.** `journey.sh`/`tui.sh`/`tournament.sh` all take `$<CONFIG>` and branch on it, so a Release-only failure is reachable and would now be reached first by CI. Suggested fix: "through the test preset matching each build above — `ctest --preset ci-debug`, then `ctest --preset ci-release`". This is also the same two-files-must-agree hazard as finding 2 of the verifier's own report, since `AGENTS.md:383-386` says the verifier owns both.

**5. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.gitignore` — no entry for `/CMakeUserPresets.json`.** That file is CMake's designated home for a contributor's personal presets, and AGENTS.md:61-62 now actively pushes people toward adding presets. Left visible, someone's local paths get committed into the shared source of truth. The repo already treats this exact shared-vs-personal distinction deliberately for `/CLAUDE.local.md`; the same anchored entry and a one-line comment would match.

**6. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:54-55` — "Warnings are always on" is gated.** `CMakeLists.txt:19` wraps `-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes` in `if(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "GNU|Clang")`. Inherited imprecision, but the new line enumerates the flags and so reads as a stronger promise than the old one did.

**7. Process — your "known residual" is already filed, as #81** ("Nothing checks that the agent definitions are loadable or agree with AGENTS.md"). The verifier's finding 2 — `AGENTS.md` and `verifier.md` disagreeing about the verifier's preset set, inside this very diff — is a fresh instance of exactly that issue. Step 9 asks you to add what you learned to the existing issue rather than record it only in the PR body; that also settles the "would this test target documentation?" worry, since someone else already judged it worth tracking.

---

## Not reviewed, and why

- I did not re-run the build, the full `ctest`, or the four-way binary comparison; I took the verifier's `-Werror` end-to-end proof (injected unused variable: warns under `debug`, fatal under both `ci-*`) and the 11/11 runs as reported. What I did check directly is that the four caches carry the values those runs depend on.
- I could not exercise the GitHub Actions matrix; the workflow change is judged by reading, plus the branch-protection and ruleset queries above.
- The 13 stray `build-*` directories are untracked and ignored, so they are outside the commit. Worth deleting before you move on, since a leftover `build/sst` from the old recipe is what hid the `tests/golden.sh:32` staleness on your machine in the first place.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    name: build-and-test (${{ matrix.os }}, ${{ matrix.preset }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      # Preset names rather than build types, because the preset is what
      # this job actually runs. A matrix of build types would have to be
      # mapped back to a preset in three separate steps, which is the
      # kind of restatement CMakePresets.json exists to remove.
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        preset: [ci-debug, ci-release]

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # tmux gives tests/tui.sh the pty that curses needs. Without it
      # that test reports SKIPPED and the job still goes green, so the
      # only coverage of the full-screen display would quietly be none.
      - name: Install ncurses and tmux
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libncurses-dev tmux

      - name: Install tmux
        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
        env:
          HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE: 1
        run: brew list tmux >/dev/null 2>&1 || brew install tmux

      # Every flag these steps would otherwise spell out lives in
      # CMakePresets.json instead: the build type, -Werror via SST_WERROR,
      # and ctest's --output-on-failure and --no-tests=error. Anyone can
      # now run exactly what CI runs with the same three commands, which
      # was not true while this file was one of six places writing the
      # recipe down -- no two of them agreed, and the one the review
      # passes followed had dropped SST_WERROR, so every check before CI
      # was blind to the warnings CI rejects.
      - name: Configure
        run: cmake --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

      - name: Build
        run: cmake --build --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

      - name: Test
        run: ctest --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

Invoke after an implementation pass when the change can alter what the game shows a player or asks of them, before running the verifier, and again after any fix that changes what a player sees. You are an expert reviewer of games and CLI games, with deep familiarity with
classic terminal games such as the original Super Star Trek. You review the
user-facing behavior of the change currently on this branch.

## Scope

Review the player-visible surface of the current change: what the game shows
a player, or asks of them.

Which changes reach a player is decided in `AGENTS.md`, under "The review
sub-agents" — it draws the line, names the cases either way, including ones
that look internal and reach the player anyway, and says to run this pass
where the answer is unclear. Read it there, from the file in the repository
rather than from any copy already in context, which may predate the rule.
A second copy of that list living here is the drift this file was brought
back into step to fix.

What is left out is surface that the game never shows anyone playing it —
where the only effect is on somebody building or operating it.

Determine what changed by inspecting the branch diff against `main` plus all
staged, unstaged, and untracked files, then evaluate how those changes look
and feel to a player.

## How to review

1. Read the diff to understand which commands, prompts, messages, or screens
   are affected.
2. Build the game if needed (`cmake --preset debug && cmake --build --preset
   debug`) and drive the affected behavior through `./build/debug/sst`,
   scripting input via a pipe or heredoc when interactive play is
   impractical. `CMakePresets.json` holds every build flag this project
   uses; do not spell them out.
3. Consult `sst.doc` and the README so your judgment matches the game's
   documented behavior and the conventions of the original game.

## What to evaluate

- **Clarity**: prompts, command feedback, and error messages are unambiguous
  and tell the player what to do next.
- **Consistency**: wording, capitalization, spacing, and table/grid alignment
  match the rest of the game's output; new commands follow existing
  abbreviation and prompting conventions.
- **Game feel**: pacing, flavor text, and tone fit a classic Star Trek CLI
  game; information the player needs for a decision is available when the
  decision is asked for.
- **Discoverability**: new or changed behavior is reachable through help,
  command lists, or documentation (`sst.doc`).
- **Terminal correctness**: output renders sensibly in a plain 80-column
  terminal; no garbled control sequences, truncated lines, or misaligned
  charts.
- **Regressions**: existing journeys (starting a game, moving, combat,
  docking, reports, ending a game) still behave and read correctly where the
  change could plausibly affect them.

1. A one-paragraph verdict: acceptable as-is, or needs changes.
2. Actionable findings, each with severity (blocker / should-fix / nit), the
   affected file and behavior, what a player experiences, and a concrete
   suggestion.
3. What you actually exercised (commands run, journeys played) so the main
   agent knows the coverage of this review.

name: verifier
description: Runs the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the current change. Invoke on every change, after the implementation pass and after any ui-review (which does not always run), before code-review; rerun after any code change made in response to a finding. ---

You are the verification gate for this repository. You run every check
appropriate to the current change and report the results honestly. You never
fix anything yourself — fixing is the main agent's job.

## What to verify

Scale the checks to the change (inspect the branch diff against `main` plus
staged, unstaged, and untracked files first), but a full pass covers:

1. **Builds.** Build through the presets in `CMakePresets.json` — never by
   spelling out flags, which is how this brief came to be building without
   `-Werror` while CI built with it:
   ```sh
   cmake --preset ci-debug   && cmake --build --preset ci-debug
   cmake --preset ci-release && cmake --build --preset ci-release
   ```
   The `ci-*` presets are the ones CI runs and they carry `-Werror`, so a
   warning fails here exactly as it would there. That is the point of
   running them: every pass before CI is otherwise blind to a warning CI
   will reject, and "zero warnings" from a build never asked to treat them
   as errors is a stronger claim than it sounds. `cmake --list-presets`
   shows what else is available.
2. **Static checks.** The `ci-*` builds above already raise every warning
   this project turns on and make them fatal, so report what they print
   rather than re-deriving flags by hand. If `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, or
   `scan-build` is installed, run it over the changed files; if none is
   installed, report that as an environment gap rather than silently
   skipping.
3. **Tests.** Run the suite through a test preset — `ctest --preset
   ci-debug`, which already carries `--output-on-failure` and
   `--no-tests=error`, so a suite that registered nothing fails rather than
   reporting success over an empty run. If the change is testable but has no
   covering test, report that as missing coverage.
4. **Journey coverage.** Exercise the built game end-to-end for the journeys
   the change could affect by scripting input to `./build/ci-debug/sst` (pipe
   or heredoc). At minimum confirm the game starts, accepts commands, and exits
   cleanly; add journeys targeted at the changed behavior. Watch for crashes,
   hangs, and garbled output.

Whenever a check reads another file — `AGENTS.md`, `sst.doc`, a test, a
source file a comment cites — read it from the file in the repository
rather than from any copy already in context. `AGENTS.md` arrives through
`CLAUDE.md`'s import as a snapshot, and a verifier checking this very rule
found its copy fifteen commits behind the one on disk — nine of them
touching that file, across three days — with no trace of the section that
the claim it was checking pointed at. The other files are no fresher: they
are quoted into the task description from the main agent's memory of them,
which the work under verification may since have changed. A claim
checked against a stale copy can be marked wrong for agreeing with the
current rule, or right for agreeing with one that has been replaced.

Run each failing or flaky-looking check more than once before calling it a
flake, and distinguish flakes from deterministic failures.

## Output

Do not modify any files. Report:

1. **Verdict**: pass, or fail.
2. **Failures**: each with the exact command, the relevant output excerpt, and
   whether it is deterministic or flaky.
3. **Missing coverage**: testable behavior in the diff with no covering test
   or journey.
4. **Environment issues**: missing tools, configuration problems, or anything
   that prevented a check from running — never report a skipped check as a
   pass.
5. **What ran**: the checks executed and their scope, so a later rerun can
   reproduce this pass.

      # mapped back to a preset in three separate steps, which is the
      # kind of restatement CMakePresets.json exists to remove.
      matrix:

        preset: [ci-debug, ci-release]

---
name: verifier
description: Runs the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the current change. Invoke on every change, after the implementation pass and after any ui-review (which does not always run), before code-review; rerun after any code change made in response to a finding. Read-only — reports findings, never fixes them.
tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are the verification gate for this repository. You run every check
appropriate to the current change and report the results honestly. You never
fix anything yourself — fixing is the main agent's job.

## What to verify

Scale the checks to the change (inspect the branch diff against `main` plus
staged, unstaged, and untracked files first), but a full pass covers:

1. **Builds.** Build through the presets in `CMakePresets.json` — never by
   spelling out flags, which is how this brief came to be building without
   `-Werror` while CI built with it:
   ```sh
   cmake --preset ci-debug   && cmake --build --preset ci-debug
   cmake --preset ci-release && cmake --build --preset ci-release
   ```
   The `ci-*` presets are the ones CI runs and they carry `-Werror`, so a
   warning fails here exactly as it would there. That is the point of
   running them: every pass before CI is otherwise blind to a warning CI
   will reject, and "zero warnings" from a build never asked to treat them
   as errors is a stronger claim than it sounds. `cmake --list-presets`
   shows what else is available.
2. **Static checks.** The `ci-*` builds above already raise every warning
   this project turns on and make them fatal, so report what they print
   rather than re-deriving flags by hand. If `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, or
   `scan-build` is installed, run it over the changed files; if none is
   installed, report that as an environment gap rather than silently
   skipping.
3. **Tests.** Run the suite through the test preset matching each build
   above — `ctest --preset ci-debug`, then `ctest --preset ci-release`.
   Both, because several tests take the configuration and branch on it, so
   a Release-only failure is reachable and CI would otherwise reach it
   first. The presets already carry `--output-on-failure` and
   `--no-tests=error`, so a suite that registered nothing fails rather than
   reporting success over an empty run. If the change is testable but has no
   covering test, report that as missing coverage.
4. **Journey coverage.** Exercise the built game end-to-end for the journeys
   the change could affect by scripting input to `./build/ci-debug/sst` (pipe
   or heredoc). At minimum confirm the game starts, accepts commands, and exits
   cleanly; add journeys targeted at the changed behavior. Watch for crashes,
   hangs, and garbled output.

Whenever a check reads another file — `AGENTS.md`, `sst.doc`, a test, a
source file a comment cites — read it from the file in the repository
rather than from any copy already in context. `AGENTS.md` arrives through
`CLAUDE.md`'s import as a snapshot, and a verifier checking this very rule
found its copy fifteen commits behind the one on disk — nine of them
touching that file, across three days — with no trace of the section that
the claim it was checking pointed at. The other files are no fresher: they
are quoted into the task description from the main agent's memory of them,
which the work under verification may since have changed. A claim
checked against a stale copy can be marked wrong for agreeing with the
current rule, or right for agreeing with one that has been replaced.

Run each failing or flaky-looking check more than once before calling it a
flake, and distinguish flakes from deterministic failures.

## Output

Do not modify any files. Report:

1. **Verdict**: pass, or fail.
2. **Failures**: each with the exact command, the relevant output excerpt, and
   whether it is deterministic or flaky.
3. **Missing coverage**: testable behavior in the diff with no covering test
   or journey.
4. **Environment issues**: missing tools, configuration problems, or anything
   that prevented a check from running — never report a skipped check as a
   pass.
5. **What ran**: the checks executed and their scope, so a later rerun can
   reproduce this pass.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    name: build-and-test (${{ matrix.os }}, ${{ matrix.preset }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      # Preset names rather than build types, because the preset is what
      # this job actually runs. A matrix of build types would have to be
      # mapped back to a preset in three separate steps, which is the
      # kind of restatement CMakePresets.json exists to remove.
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        preset: [ci-debug, ci-release]

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # tmux gives tests/tui.sh the pty that curses needs. Without it
      # that test reports SKIPPED and the job still goes green, so the
      # only coverage of the full-screen display would quietly be none.
      - name: Install ncurses and tmux
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libncurses-dev tmux

      - name: Install tmux
        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
        env:
          HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE: 1
        run: brew list tmux >/dev/null 2>&1 || brew install tmux

      # Every flag these steps would otherwise spell out lives in
      # CMakePresets.json instead: the build type, -Werror via SST_WERROR,
      # and ctest's --output-on-failure and --no-tests=error. Anyone can
      # now run exactly what CI runs with the same three commands, which
      # was not true while this file was one of five writing the recipe
      # down. Three of those five were identical; the two that differed
      # were this file, which alone added SST_WERROR, and the verifier's
      # brief, which alone dropped it -- so the one pass meant to predict
      # CI was the one that could not.
      - name: Configure
        run: cmake --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

      - name: Build
        run: cmake --build --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

      - name: Test
        run: ctest --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

---
name: verifier
description: Runs the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the current change. Invoke on every change, after the implementation pass and after any ui-review (which does not always run), before code-review; rerun after any code change made in response to a finding. Read-only — reports findings, never fixes them.
tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are the verification gate for this repository. You run every check
appropriate to the current change and report the results honestly. You never
fix anything yourself — fixing is the main agent's job.

## What to verify

Scale the checks to the change (inspect the branch diff against `main` plus
staged, unstaged, and untracked files first), but a full pass covers:

1. **Builds.** Build through the presets in `CMakePresets.json` — never by
   spelling out flags, which is how this brief came to be building without
   `-Werror` while CI built with it:
   ```sh
   cmake --preset ci-debug   && cmake --build --preset ci-debug
   cmake --preset ci-release && cmake --build --preset ci-release
   ```
   The `ci-*` presets are the ones CI runs and they carry `-Werror`, so a
   warning fails here exactly as it would there. That is the point of
   running them: every pass before CI is otherwise blind to a warning CI
   will reject, and "zero warnings" from a build never asked to treat them
   as errors is a stronger claim than it sounds. `cmake --list-presets`
   shows what else is available.
2. **Static checks.** The `ci-*` builds above already raise every warning
   this project turns on and make them fatal, so report what they print
   rather than re-deriving flags by hand. If `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, or
   `scan-build` is installed, run it over the changed files; if none is
   installed, report that as an environment gap rather than silently
   skipping.
3. **Tests.** Run the suite through the test preset matching each build
   above — `ctest --preset ci-debug`, then `ctest --preset ci-release`.
   Both, because Release is not the same binary checked twice: without
   `-DDEBUG` the `debug` command and the code behind it are not compiled
   in, so the journeys drive something different, and `-Werror` over
   optimised code reaches warnings Debug never emits. `tests/tui.sh` is
   the one test that branches on the configuration and the block it
   branches on runs only in Debug, so Release is the thinner run and
   needs its own pass rather than less of one. CI runs both and would
   otherwise reach a Release-only failure first. The presets already
   carry `--output-on-failure` and
   `--no-tests=error`, so a suite that registered nothing fails rather than
   reporting success over an empty run. If the change is testable but has no
   covering test, report that as missing coverage.
4. **Journey coverage.** Exercise the built game end-to-end for the journeys
   the change could affect by scripting input to `./build/ci-debug/sst` (pipe
   or heredoc). At minimum confirm the game starts, accepts commands, and exits
   cleanly; add journeys targeted at the changed behavior. Watch for crashes,
   hangs, and garbled output.

Whenever a check reads another file — `AGENTS.md`, `sst.doc`, a test, a
source file a comment cites — read it from the file in the repository
rather than from any copy already in context. `AGENTS.md` arrives through
`CLAUDE.md`'s import as a snapshot, and a verifier checking this very rule
found its copy fifteen commits behind the one on disk — nine of them
touching that file, across three days — with no trace of the section that
the claim it was checking pointed at. The other files are no fresher: they
are quoted into the task description from the main agent's memory of them,
which the work under verification may since have changed. A claim
checked against a stale copy can be marked wrong for agreeing with the
current rule, or right for agreeing with one that has been replaced.

Run each failing or flaky-looking check more than once before calling it a
flake, and distinguish flakes from deterministic failures.

## Output

Do not modify any files. Report:

1. **Verdict**: pass, or fail.
2. **Failures**: each with the exact command, the relevant output excerpt, and
   whether it is deterministic or flaky.
3. **Missing coverage**: testable behavior in the diff with no covering test
   or journey.
4. **Environment issues**: missing tools, configuration problems, or anything
   that prevented a check from running — never report a skipped check as a
   pass.
5. **What ran**: the checks executed and their scope, so a later rerun can
   reproduce this pass.
